modules.title: Control plane and lifecycle
modules.summary: API server, etcd, certificates and kubeadm upgrades.

lessons.title: Control plane internals: API server, etcd and certificates
lessons.summary: Follow a request through authentication, authorization and admission, back up and restore etcd, and keep cluster certificates valid.
objectives: Trace an API request through authn, authz, mutating and validating admission and persistence
Take and verify an etcd snapshot, and know the restore procedure
Explain what the controller manager and scheduler do and how they cooperate
Inspect and renew control plane certificates with kubeadm

sections.title: Everything goes through the API server
sections.body:
The **kube-apiserver** is the only component that talks to etcd. Every other part (scheduler, controller manager, kubelets, kubectl) is a client of the API server and watches resources for changes. This design makes the API server the single place where security, validation and auditing are enforced.

A write request passes a fixed pipeline: **authentication** (who are you), **authorization** (may you do this), **mutating admission** (webhooks and built-in plugins may modify the object), **schema validation**, **validating admission** (policies and webhooks may reject it) and finally **persistence** to etcd. Reads skip the admission stages.

The **kube-controller-manager** runs reconcile loops (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node, Job, EndpointSlice and more). Each loop watches desired state and acts to close the gap. The **scheduler** only assigns unscheduled Pods to nodes by writing `spec.nodeName`; the kubelet does the rest. Both use **leader election** via Lease objects, so only one replica is active.

kubeadm issues certificates valid for **one year** (the CA for ten). They renew automatically during `kubeadm upgrade`, but a cluster that is never upgraded will stop working on expiry. Check with `kubeadm certs check-expiration` and monitor the date.

sections.title: About this example: a kubeadm static Pod manifest for the API server
sections.body: This fragment is what `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` contains on a kubeadm control plane node. The kubelet watches that directory and runs the file as a **static Pod**, so editing it restarts the API server. Look at `--authorization-mode`, `--enable-admission-plugins` and the `--etcd-*` flags: they define the pipeline stages and the path to etcd. It is a partial file, so it is shown as text and not applied with kubectl.

sections.title: kube-apiserver flags (excerpt)
sections.note: Authorization modes are evaluated in order; the first that allows wins. Node handles kubelets, RBAC handles everyone else.

sections.title: About this example: snapshotting etcd
sections.body: etcd holds all cluster state, so a snapshot is your disaster recovery backup. These commands run on a control plane node using `etcdctl` with the client certificates kubeadm generated. `snapshot save` writes a consistent point-in-time file and `snapshot status` verifies it; check the hash and total key count in the table output. Store the file off the node and test restores regularly. The second half of the block restores that snapshot into a fresh data directory, which you do with the API server stopped and then point the etcd manifest at the new path.

sections.title: etcdctl backup, verify and restore
sections.code:
export ETCDCTL_API=3
ETCD_FLAGS="--endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key"
etcdctl $ETCD_FLAGS snapshot save /backup/etcd-$(date +%F).db
etcdctl --write-out=table snapshot status /backup/etcd-$(date +%F).db
mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/
etcdutl snapshot restore /backup/etcd-2026-11-13.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restored
sed -i 's#/var/lib/etcd$#/var/lib/etcd-restored#' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
mv /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
kubectl get nodes

sections.title: About this example: checking and renewing certificates
sections.body: These commands run on the control plane node. `check-expiration` lists every certificate and its remaining time, and `renew all` reissues them; afterwards the static Pods must restart to load the new files. Watch the RESIDUAL TIME column and EXTERNALLY MANAGED, which tells you if kubeadm is allowed to touch a certificate.

sections.title: Restore rewinds the whole cluster
sections.body: Anything created after the snapshot (Deployments, Secrets, PVC bindings) disappears, while running containers on nodes are unaware. In multi-member etcd you must restore every member from the same snapshot with new `--initial-cluster` settings. Practice this in a throwaway cluster before you need it.

questions.question: A request is denied with 403 after authentication succeeded. Which stage most likely rejected it?
questions.explain: 401 means authentication failed; 403 comes from authorization or an admission rejection.

questions.question: Which component is the only one that reads and writes etcd directly?
questions.explain: All other components use the API server, which centralizes security and validation.

questions.question: Why must the API server be stopped during an etcd restore?
options: To avoid writes into a data directory being replaced
questions.explain: Writes during the swap would be lost or corrupt state; stopping it gives a clean cutover.

questions.question: kubeadm client certificates are valid for how long by default?
questions.explain: Leaf certificates last one year and are renewed on kubeadm upgrade; the CA lasts ten years.

lessons.title: Cluster lifecycle with kubeadm: install, skew policy and upgrades
lessons.summary: Bootstrap a cluster with kubeadm, respect the version skew policy and run a safe control plane and node upgrade.
objectives: Describe what kubeadm init and join do
Apply the version skew policy to plan upgrades
Run an ordered upgrade of control plane then workers
Define rollback and verification steps

sections.title: What kubeadm does and does not do
sections.body:
**kubeadm** bootstraps a minimum viable cluster: it generates certificates, writes static Pod manifests for the control plane, creates kubeconfigs and bootstrap tokens, and installs CoreDNS and kube-proxy. It does not install a CNI plugin, a load balancer, storage or the container runtime. You provide those.

A production setup uses a **ClusterConfiguration** file so the whole install is declarative, versioned in Git and repeatable. A stable `controlPlaneEndpoint` (a load balancer or virtual IP) is essential for adding control plane nodes later. After `kubeadm init` prints a join command with a token and CA hash, run it on each new node; add `--control-plane` for extra API server nodes. Always upgrade one minor version at a time: skipping minors breaks the skew policy, and you should check deprecated API usage first.

sections.title: About this example: a kubeadm configuration file
sections.body: This is the file you pass to `kubeadm init --config`. It fixes the Kubernetes version, the Pod and Service CIDRs and the API endpoint at install time, which are painful to change afterwards. Look at `controlPlaneEndpoint` (use a stable DNS name), `podSubnet` (must match your CNI) and `certSANs`. It has multiple YAML documents with custom kinds that kubectl cannot apply, so it is shown as text.

sections.title: kubeadm-config.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta4
kind: InitConfiguration
nodeRegistration:
  criSocket: unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock
---
apiVersion: kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta4
kind: ClusterConfiguration
kubernetesVersion: v1.33.2
controlPlaneEndpoint: k8s-api.example.com:6443
networking:
  podSubnet: 10.244.0.0/16
  serviceSubnet: 10.96.0.0/12
apiServer:
  certSANs:
  - k8s-api.example.com
---
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
cgroupDriver: systemd

sections.title: About this example: the control plane upgrade runbook
sections.body: These commands run on the first control plane node. `kubeadm upgrade plan` verifies the cluster, shows available versions and the component diff, and `upgrade apply` performs the change and renews certificates. Afterwards upgrade the kubelet package and restart it on that node. Look at the plan's 'COMPONENT CURRENT TARGET' table to confirm only expected versions change.

sections.title: Upgrade the first control plane node
sections.code:
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.33.2-1.1
sudo kubeadm upgrade plan
sudo kubeadm upgrade apply v1.33.2
kubectl drain cp1 --ignore-daemonsets
sudo apt-get install -y kubelet=1.33.2-1.1 kubectl=1.33.2-1.1
sudo systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl uncordon cp1

sections.title: About this example: upgrading a worker node
sections.body: Workers are upgraded one at a time (or in small batches limited by PodDisruptionBudgets). You drain the node from a machine with kubectl, then run `kubeadm upgrade node` on the worker itself and upgrade the kubelet. Check VERSION in `kubectl get nodes` afterwards; a node showing the old version has not restarted its kubelet.

sections.title: Worker upgrade loop
sections.code:
kubectl drain w1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
# on w1:
sudo apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.33.2-1.1
sudo kubeadm upgrade node
sudo apt-get install -y kubelet=1.33.2-1.1
sudo systemctl restart kubelet
# back on the admin machine:
kubectl uncordon w1
kubectl get nodes

lessons.title: Networking internals: CNI, kube-proxy and DNS
lessons.summary: See how Pod networking is built by CNI plugins, how kube-proxy programs Services, and how to tune cluster DNS.
objectives: Explain the role of the CNI plugin and Pod-to-Pod paths
Compare iptables, IPVS and eBPF Service data paths
Read kube-proxy iptables rules and EndpointSlices
Tune CoreDNS and Pod DNS settings

sections.title: CNI and the Pod network
sections.body:
When the kubelet starts a Pod, the container runtime creates the network namespace and calls the **CNI plugin** configured in `/etc/cni/net.d`. The plugin creates a veth pair, attaches one end to the Pod, assigns an IP from the node's Pod CIDR and sets up routes. The Kubernetes model requires that every Pod can reach every other Pod without NAT.

Plugins differ in how cross-node traffic travels. **Overlay** (VXLAN, Geneve) encapsulates packets and works anywhere. **Routed** (BGP, native cloud routing) avoids encapsulation for better performance. Cilium and Calico can also enforce NetworkPolicy and replace kube-proxy.

**kube-proxy** watches Services and EndpointSlices and programs the node. In **iptables mode** it writes NAT rules with random probability to pick a backend; rule evaluation is linear, so clusters with tens of thousands of Services slow down. **IPVS mode** uses kernel hash tables for O(1) lookup and offers schedulers like round robin and least connection. **nftables mode** is the modern successor of iptables. **eBPF** (Cilium) replaces kube-proxy entirely with kernel programs attached to sockets and interfaces, avoiding conntrack for many flows.

How it works
Notes
rows: veth to bridge or direct route inside the node
Node routes via BGP or cloud route table
DNAT to a backend Pod IP by kube-proxy or eBPF
ClusterIP is virtual, never on an interface

sections.title: About this example: a CNI configuration file
sections.body: This is a typical conflist file in `/etc/cni/net.d/` read by the runtime to chain plugins. Look at `type` (the plugin binary in `/opt/cni/bin`), `ipam` (where Pod IPs come from) and `mtu`. A wrong MTU on overlays causes the classic 'small requests work, large ones hang' failure. It is a node file, not a Kubernetes object, so it is shown as text.

sections.title: /etc/cni/net.d/10-flannel.conflist
sections.note: Other plugins use their own files, e.g. 05-cilium.conflist.

sections.title: About this example: EndpointSlices and kube-proxy rules
sections.body: This block shows the Service-to-backend path in two views. `kubectl get endpointslices` lists the ready Pod IPs the control plane tracks for the `web` Service (selector app=web, port 80 to targetPort 8080), and `iptables-save` on a node shows how kube-proxy converts them to rules. Follow the chain: `KUBE-SERVICES` matches the ClusterIP, jumps to a `KUBE-SVC-` chain, which picks a `KUBE-SEP-` chain by probability, which DNATs to a Pod IP. Look at the `--probability` lines: with three backends the first gets 0.33 and the second 0.5 of the remainder.

sections.title: Endpoints and iptables NAT rules
sections.code:
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web
sudo iptables-save -t nat | grep -E 'default/web'

sections.title: About this example: tuning DNS for a Pod
sections.body: By default Pods get `ndots:5`, so a lookup of `api.example.com` first tries several cluster search domains, multiplying queries. This Pod lowers `ndots` and adds an option, which cuts external lookup latency. Check `dnsConfig` and then run the Pod's `cat /etc/resolv.conf` to see the effect.

sections.title: Pod with dnsConfig
sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: dns-tuned
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
  dnsConfig:
    options:
    - name: ndots
      value: "2"
    - name: single-request-reopen

sections.title: Scale DNS deliberately
sections.body: Run NodeLocal DNSCache to cut CoreDNS load and conntrack pressure, scale CoreDNS with the cluster-proportional-autoscaler, and use fully qualified names ending in a dot for hot external lookups.

questions.explain: IPVS uses hash tables and eBPF avoids per-rule traversal.

lessons.title: Storage internals: CSI, snapshots, expansion and topology
lessons.summary: Understand how CSI drivers provision and attach volumes, and use snapshots, expansion and topology-aware binding.
objectives: Describe the CSI controller and node plugin roles
Create and restore VolumeSnapshots
Expand a PVC online
Use WaitForFirstConsumer for topology-aware provisioning

sections.title: How CSI works
sections.body:
The **Container Storage Interface** lets storage vendors ship drivers without changing Kubernetes. A driver has two parts. The **controller plugin** (a Deployment with sidecars such as external-provisioner, external-attacher, external-snapshotter and external-resizer) talks to the storage API to create, attach and snapshot volumes. The **node plugin** (a DaemonSet) mounts and formats volumes on the node when the kubelet asks.

The flow is: a PVC references a StorageClass, the provisioner creates the volume and a PV, the attacher binds it to a node (VolumeAttachment), and the kubelet calls NodeStage/NodePublish to mount it into the Pod.

sections.title: StorageClass fields that matter
head: Field
Meaning
Example
rows: Delete or Retain on PVC removal

sections.title: About this example: a topology-aware StorageClass
sections.body: This StorageClass uses `WaitForFirstConsumer`, so the volume is created only after the scheduler picks a node. That ensures the volume lands in the same zone as the Pod, avoiding the unschedulable 'volume node affinity conflict'. Apply it with kubectl; check `volumeBindingMode` and `allowVolumeExpansion`.

sections.title: StorageClass fast-zonal
sections.code:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: fast-zonal
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Delete
parameters:
  type: gp3
  encrypted: "true"

sections.title: About this example: expanding a volume
sections.body: Growing a volume means editing the PVC request to a larger value; the external-resizer grows the backing disk and the kubelet resizes the filesystem, usually while the Pod runs. Use `kubectl patch` and then watch the PVC conditions. Volumes can only grow, never shrink.

sections.title: Expand a PVC
sections.code:
kubectl patch pvc data-db-0 -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"50Gi"}}}}'
kubectl get pvc data-db-0
sections.output:
persistentvolumeclaim/data-db-0 patched
NAME        STATUS   VOLUME      CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS   AGE
data-db-0   Bound    pvc-8a1f   50Gi       RWO            fast-zonal     12d

sections.title: About this example: a VolumeSnapshot
sections.body: This block holds two manifests applied together. The VolumeSnapshot names the source PVC and a VolumeSnapshotClass tied to the driver; `kubectl get volumesnapshot` must show READYTOUSE true before a restore. The PVC then uses `dataSource` pointing to the snapshot, so the provisioner creates a volume pre-populated with its data; the requested size must be at least the snapshot size.

sections.title: VolumeSnapshot and restored PVC
sections.code:
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshot
metadata:
  name: db-snap-1
spec:
  volumeSnapshotClassName: ebs-snapclass
  source:
    persistentVolumeClaimName: data-db-0
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: data-db-restored
spec:
  storageClassName: fast-zonal
  dataSource:
    name: db-snap-1
    kind: VolumeSnapshot
    apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi

sections.title: Snapshots are not backups by themselves
sections.body: Most snapshots live in the same storage system and failure domain as the volume. Combine them with application-consistent quiescing (for example a database flush) and copy data off-cluster with a tool such as Velero for real disaster recovery.

questions.explain: The volume is provisioned after scheduling so it is in the Pod's zone.

questions.explain: The node plugin runs on every node and performs stage and publish.

modules.title: Multi-tenancy and fleets
modules.summary: Isolation models and managing many clusters.

lessons.title: Multi-cluster, multi-tenancy and fleet management
lessons.summary: Choose between namespaces, virtual clusters and separate clusters, enforce per-tenant limits and manage many clusters as a fleet.
objectives: Compare isolation levels of namespaces, vclusters and clusters
Apply quotas, limits and policies per tenant
Describe federation and GitOps fleet patterns
Pick a tenancy model from requirements

sections.title: Three tenancy models
sections.body:
**Namespace per tenant** is the cheapest: tenants share the control plane and nodes, and isolation comes from RBAC, ResourceQuota, NetworkPolicy and Pod Security. It suits trusted teams in one company. **Virtual clusters** (vcluster) give each tenant their own API server and control plane data running as Pods inside a host cluster, so tenants can install CRDs and cluster-scoped objects safely, while sharing worker nodes. **Cluster per tenant** gives the strongest isolation at the highest cost and operational load.

The key trade-off is blast radius versus overhead. Shared control planes mean one noisy tenant can exhaust API server capacity, and a kernel escape affects all tenants on a node.

Beyond one cluster, teams want consistent configuration and workload placement. Classic **KubeFed** (federation v2) has been archived; today the common patterns are **GitOps fleets** (Argo CD ApplicationSets or Flux with a cluster per directory), **Cluster API** for declarative cluster lifecycle, and **multi-cluster services** (MCS API, Cilium ClusterMesh) for cross-cluster discovery. Group clusters by environment and region, promote changes through them, and keep a single policy source such as Kyverno or Gatekeeper bundles applied everywhere.

sections.title: About this example: a tenant namespace with a quota
sections.body: This single file onboards a tenant: a Namespace labelled for Pod Security `restricted`, a RoleBinding granting the built-in `edit` ClusterRole to the tenant group only inside that namespace, a ResourceQuota capping CPU, memory, Pods and PVCs, and a default-deny NetworkPolicy (needs a CNI that enforces policy). Apply with kubectl in one step; look at `roleRef` versus `subjects`, the `hard` limits and the empty `podSelector` that matches every Pod.

sections.title: Tenant onboarding bundle
sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: team-a
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    tenant: team-a
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: team-a-editors
  namespace: team-a
subjects:
- kind: Group
  name: team-a-developers
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: edit
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-a-quota
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "20"
    requests.memory: 64Gi
    limits.cpu: "40"
    limits.memory: 128Gi
    pods: "100"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "20"
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
sections.output:
namespace/team-a created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/team-a-editors created
resourcequota/team-a-quota created
networkpolicy.networking.k8s.io/default-deny-all created

sections.title: About this example: checking tenant usage
sections.body: After the quota exists, this command shows consumed versus allowed resources. The USED column should never exceed HARD; once a limit is reached, new Pods are rejected with a 'exceeded quota' error.

sections.title: Inspect quota usage
sections.output:
Name:                   team-a-quota
Namespace:              team-a
Resource                Used   Hard
--------                ----   ----
limits.cpu              12     40
limits.memory           24Gi   128Gi
persistentvolumeclaims  4      20
pods                    18     100
requests.cpu            6      20
requests.memory         12Gi   64Gi

sections.title: Hierarchical namespaces and policy as code
sections.body: Use admission policies (ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, Kyverno) to require tenant labels, quotas and registries consistently. Treat tenant onboarding as code: one pull request creates the namespace, quota, RBAC and network policy.

questions.question: Which model lets a tenant install their own CRDs without affecting others?
questions.explain: Tenants with their own API server can manage cluster-scoped resources safely.

questions.question: What does an empty podSelector in a NetworkPolicy mean?
questions.explain: An empty selector matches every Pod in the namespace.

questions.question: What does ResourceQuota prevent?
options: One namespace consuming unbounded shared capacity
questions.explain: Quotas cap aggregate consumption per namespace.

questions.question: Which approach is recommended today for syncing config across clusters?
questions.explain: KubeFed is archived; GitOps fleet patterns are the common choice.
